name: Microneedling (SkinPen)

lead: SkinPen is an electric microneedling device used by clinicians for acne scars, wrinkles and overall skin texture, for smoother skin and softer scars.

Tiny punctures are thought to trigger skin repair and collagen remodelling, which is the standard description of microneedling. Registered SkinPen trials cover neck wrinkles, acne scars on the face and back, acne, hand aging and vitiligo; no results were summarised in the sources reviewed.

paras: It is done in a clinic in a series of sessions, sometimes combined with platelet-rich plasma. Results build gradually as skin remodels.
Infection is a documented risk in untrained or non-sterile settings, including a 2024 CDC report tied to a spa facial procedure. It is commonly described as FDA-cleared when used by clinicians.

angle.text: It is used for acne scars, wrinkles and overall texture: tiny punctures trigger repair and collagen remodelling, leading to smoother skin and softer scars. It is sometimes combined with platelet-rich plasma, and several small SkinPen trials are registered.

lead: Microneedling, also called collagen induction therapy, skin needling or dermarolling, is a cosmetic procedure in which many fine, sterile needles repeatedly puncture the skin's surface.[1][2] The aim is to leave the epidermis largely intact while the small channels trigger the skin's repair response, which reviews describe as growth-factor release and new collagen production.[2] People use it to soften the look of acne scars, stretch marks and fine lines, to even out skin texture, to improve the appearance of aging skin and, in combination with other products, for hair loss and facial hair.[1][2][3]

SkinPen is a branded electric microneedling pen used in a series of registered clinical studies on wrinkles, acne scars, acne, hand aging and vitiligo.[4][5][6][7][8] The category it belongs to includes manual rollers and stamps sold for home use, motorised pens such as the SkinPen and Dermapen used in clinics, and radiofrequency microneedling devices that add heat energy through the needles.[2][9]

A 2017 comprehensive review in Dermatologic Surgery concluded that studies show efficacy and safety for scars, acne, melasma, photodamage, skin rejuvenation, hyperhidrosis and alopecia, and for helping topical products cross the skin barrier, while calling for larger randomized trials.[2] Transient redness and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation are the most commonly reported adverse effects.[2] Microneedling is also a staple of online skincare and looksmaxxing discussion, where home roller and stamp routines, needle-depth debates and combinations with tretinoin, minoxidil or peptides are common topics.[10][11][12]

paras: In collagen induction therapy a device studded with fine needles is passed over the skin, creating a dense pattern of tiny punctures. Because the needles go through the epidermis but the surface is not removed, reviewers describe the approach as minimally invasive with limited downtime compared with resurfacing lasers.[2] A review of microneedling for hair loss dates the method to the 1990s and notes that the mechanism is not fully understood, with wound-healing processes the leading explanation.[3]

The punctures are also used to create temporary channels for topical products. The 2017 review lists facilitation of transdermal drug delivery among microneedling applications, and a Wikipedia entry distinguishes this use, along with vaccination, from collagen induction itself.[1][2]

Manual devices include rollers (a drum of needles) and flat stamps, which are the tools most often discussed in home-use threads.[10][13] Electric pens drive a cartridge of needles up and down at adjustable depth and are used in clinics; the SkinPen Precision in registered studies, for instance, was applied at depths of up to 1.5 mm on the face and up to 2.5 mm on the neck.[4][6] Radiofrequency microneedling combines needles with energy delivered into the dermis; a 2021 review identified 42 higher-quality randomized, split-body or blinded studies covering skin rejuvenation, acne scars, acne, striae and other uses.[9]
Microneedling is applied to many appearance concerns. The ones with the most published material are summarised below.

Atrophic (depressed) acne scars are the best-known indication. Small studies with rollers, indexed in Europe PMC, reported shifts in scar grading: in a 31-patient Vietnamese study weekly dermaroller sessions over three months lowered average Goodman and Baron grades from 3.29 to 1.77 at two months after treatment, and a 50-patient study of facial scars graded 14% of responses excellent and 52% good.[14] A registered SkinPen study enrolled 41 adults with atrophic acne scars on the face or back and graded scars on the Goodman and Baron scale; the posted results show mean scores moving from about 3.1-3.2 at baseline to about 2.6-2.7 at six months.[5] A separate proof-of-concept SkinPen study examined inflammatory and non-inflammatory acne lesions in 31 participants.[6]

An open-label study of 48 adults aged 35 to 75 using an automated microneedling device (four sessions about a month apart) reported improvements in wrinkles, laxity and texture by day 150, with minimal pain and downtime; the authors designed it to support a US regulatory submission.[14] In a registered single-arm SkinPen study of neck wrinkles, 35 participants were treated on days 1, 30, 60 and 90; the posted results show the Lemperle wrinkle score falling from a mean of 3.31 to 2.45 at three months, and 30 of 32 respondents noticing improvement at one month.[4] Other SkinPen registrations cover hand aging (18 participants, no posted results) and dermatoporosis.[15][7]

A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of striae distensae included six randomized and five non-randomized studies; it found a significant benefit in the microneedle radiofrequency subgroup (SMD 0.57) and comparable results between microneedling and lasers.[16] For melasma, a systematic review reports that microneedling and peels were efficacious though their superiority to topical hydroquinone remains to be established, and that recurrence rates stay high across treatments.[17] A registered SkinPen study examined microneedling alone for vitiligo.[8]

A 2022 review in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology analysed trials in androgenetic alopecia and reported that microneedling alone raised hair counts more than topical 5% minoxidil in the pooled regression, and that adding minoxidil to microneedling raised counts further; the authors noted that few studies test microneedling alone and called for larger trials.[3] A 2025 meta-analysis of 12 randomized trials (631 patients) found combined microneedling plus minoxidil improved hair count versus minoxidil alone (SMD 1.32, high heterogeneity) and hair diameter (SMD 0.34), with mild adverse events more frequent in the combination arm.[14] A randomized placebo-controlled letter examined microneedling with a topical dutasteride solution, and a 2025 phase I trial examined PRP injections with microneedling.[18][19] A 2024 systematic review of androgenic alopecia treatment lists microneedling-adjacent procedural options such as PRP and fractionated lasers alongside drugs.[20] Beard and eyebrow needling is a recurring community topic.[21][22]

Microneedling is frequently paired with other treatments. Platelet-rich plasma (PRP), prepared from the patient's own blood and applied to or injected into the skin, is combined with needling in what is marketed as a vampire facial; Wikipedia states that the efficacy of the combination remains to be established by studies.[1][23] Registered studies compare microneedling with and without PRP and a fractional laser with and without microneedling for acne scars.[24][25] A 2024 randomized trial examined radiofrequency microneedling to enhance penetration of poly-L-lactic acid for facial laxity.[26]

SkinPen is an electric pen whose registered studies list Bellus Medical or Crown Laboratories as sponsor; the registered acne scar study lists two models, SkinPen II and SkinPen Precision, each used for three monthly treatments with needle depths of 0.25 to 2.0 mm.[5] Its dedicated clinical programme consists of small single-site, mostly open-label studies run in Dallas, Texas.[4][5][6][7] The acne scar study used the Goodman and Baron scar scale and a clinician global assessment, and reported no serious adverse events.[5]

Evidence ranges from randomized split-face and meta-analytic work to small open-label device studies. The 2017 review of human studies concluded that microneedling appears effective and safe across a range of conditions while calling for larger randomized trials in different skin types.[2] The registered SkinPen studies are small: 35 (neck wrinkles), 41 (acne scars), 31 (acne), 18 (hand aging) and 13 (vitiligo).[4][5][6][7][8] A hand-aging study was withdrawn before enrolment.[27] Posted results exist for the neck wrinkle and acne scar studies; the acne, hand aging and vitiligo registrations had no posted outcome data when reviewed.[4][5][6][7]

Reviews also show where findings are mixed. For striae, benefit appeared in some subgroups; for melasma, comparisons with hydroquinone are unsettled; and for hair loss, most trials combine needling with minoxidil or PRP.[16][3][17]

Reviews describe transient redness as the most common effect and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation as more frequently reported than permanent adverse events.[2] Wikipedia notes that infection control is the main concern when procedures are performed outside licensed settings.[1] In April 2024 the US CDC reported three women diagnosed with HIV after vampire facials at an unlicensed Albuquerque spa; about 200 other former clients tested negative, and investigators attributed the cluster to reuse of blood-contaminated single-use equipment.[1][23]

Home users often write about disinfecting rollers and stamps between uses and avoiding needling over active acne, as in an at-home guide thread.[10] The registered SkinPen acne scar study, which used three sessions a month apart, reported no serious adverse events.[5]

On looksmax.org, microneedling appears in beginner guides to home rollers and stamps, debates about how deep to go with a pen, and threads on pairing it with tretinoin, peptides or hair-growth topicals.[10][11][28][12][29] One thread asks whether a stamp counts as microneedling at all.[13] Others ask about the best approach for beard and eyebrow density.[21][22] A thread titled "Microneedling is bad" quotes an article arguing that collagen produced after needling is a stress response and that plumping is inflammation, and replies in the thread disagree.[21]

Depth is a recurring question: commenters in one thread suggest deeper needling is used less often because of scarring concerns and that radiofrequency microneedling from a dermatologist is an alternative.[11]

timeline.event: Microneedling introduced as a minimally invasive skin and scar treatment, per a 2022 review.[3]
SkinPen acne-scar study (41 participants) begins in Dallas.[5]
Comprehensive review in Dermatologic Surgery summarises human studies of microneedling.[2]
Open-label study of an automated microneedling device in 48 adults reports improvements in aging skin.[14]
SkinPen neck-wrinkle study (35 participants) starts; fractional laser and PRP comparison studies registered.[4][24][25]
SkinPen hand-aging and vitiligo studies start; neck-wrinkle results posted.[4][7][8]
Review of radiofrequency microneedling covers 42 higher-quality studies.[9]
Gupta and colleagues publish a review of microneedling for hair loss.[3]
CDC reports three HIV diagnoses linked to vampire facials at an Albuquerque spa; striae meta-analysis published.[1][16][23]
Meta-analysis of 12 randomized trials compares microneedling plus minoxidil with minoxidil alone.[14]
